\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The question the normalization answers}

Let $\X$ be a finite set and let $p,q$ be probability distributions on it. Two normalizations of the same underlying object compete in the literature:
\[
\|p-q\|_1=\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|,\qquad \dtv(p,q)=\frac12\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|.
\]
Both are metrics on the simplex; they differ by a constant; and it is common to treat the choice as immaterial. It is not immaterial, and this paper is an account of why.

The reason is \emph{operational}. There is a question of genuine interest --- how well can a single observation distinguish $p$ from $q$? --- and exactly one of the two normalizations answers it. An observer who sees a sample and must decide whether it came from $p$ or from $q$ has optimal advantage over guessing equal to $\dtv(p,q)$, and the optimum is achieved by an explicit test. The $\ell^1$ quantity is not the optimum of anything probabilistic; it is the optimum of a \emph{signed} variational problem over a larger, non-probabilistic class of tests. Using $\ell^1$ where $\dtv$ belongs is not a harmless constant-factor concession: it answers a coarser question and inherits the slack.

\subsection{The two faces of total variation}

The technical core is that $\dtv$ has two exact descriptions:
\begin{itemize}
\item a \emph{primal/testing} description as $\max_A(p(A)-q(A))$, witnessed by the likelihood-ratio event $A^\star=\{x:q(x)\le p(x)\}$;
\item a \emph{dual/transport} description as $\min_c\PR_c[X\neq Y]$ over couplings, witnessed by the maximal coupling.
\end{itemize}
Each is proved by exhibiting its optimum, and the two proofs are linked: the coupling lower bound is obtained by pushing the optimal \emph{event} through an arbitrary coupling. The pair constitutes a minimax identity with matching certificates; our proof is constructive rather than by linear-programming duality (see Section~\ref{sec:disc}).

\subsection{Why attainment, not validity, is the point}

A bound that is valid can be chained; a bound that is \emph{attained} can be chained without loss and audited at each step. In each application below the sharp constant is the difference between a usable statement and a vacuous one.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Statement & with $\dtv$ & with $\|\cdot\|_1$\\
\midrule
Two-point testing optimum & $(1-\dtv)/2\in[0,\tfrac12]$ & $(1-\|p-q\|_1)/2$, negative if $\|p-q\|_1>1$\\
Pinsker-derived error bound & $(1-\sqrt{\KL/2})/2$ & $(1-\sqrt{2\KL})/2$, vacuous for $\KL\in[\tfrac18,\tfrac12]$\\
Coupling identity & $\min_c\PR[X\neq Y]=\dtv\in[0,1]$ & right-hand side may exceed $1$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section{The event-supremum characterization}

\subsection{Definitions}

Throughout, $\X$ is a finite set. A \emph{law} on $\X$ is $p:\X\to\mathbb{R}$ with $p\ge0$ and $\sum_x p(x)=1$; several statements need only the normalization.

\begin{definition}[Total variation distance]
$\dtv(p,q)=\dfrac12\sum_{x\in\X}|p(x)-q(x)|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Event probability and distinguishing gap]
For $A\subseteq\X$, $p(A)=\sum_{x\in A}p(x)$ and
$\Delta_{p,q}(A)=p(A)-q(A)=\sum_{x\in A}(p(x)-q(x))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Likelihood-ratio event]
$A^\star=A^\star(p,q)=\{x\in\X: q(x)\le p(x)\}$, the Neyman--Pearson test at threshold $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Boolean and randomized advantage]
For $f:\X\to\{0,1\}$ the \emph{Boolean advantage} is $\Delta_{p,q}(f^{-1}(1))$. For $g:\X\to[0,1]$, a randomized test accepting $x$ with probability $g(x)$, the \emph{soft advantage} is $\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))g(x)$.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Event-supremum characterization]\label{thm:eventsup}
Let $p,q$ be laws on $\X$. Then $\Delta_{p,q}(A)\le\dtv(p,q)$ for every $A\subseteq\X$, with equality for $A=A^\star$. Consequently
\[
\dtv(p,q)=\max_{A\subseteq\X}\bigl(p(A)-q(A)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $u_+=\max(u,0)$. First, the \emph{surplus identity} $\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))_+=\dtv(p,q)$: since $\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))=0$, the total positive part equals the total negative part, while their sum is $\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|=2\dtv$. Second, for any $A$,
\[
\sum_{x\in A}(p(x)-q(x))\le\sum_{x\in A}(p(x)-q(x))_+\le\sum_{x\in\X}(p(x)-q(x))_+,
\]
using $u\le u_+$ termwise and non-negativity of the omitted terms. For attainment, $x\in A^\star$ iff $p(x)-q(x)\ge0$, so $\sum_{x\in A^\star}(p(x)-q(x))=\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))_+=\dtv(p,q)$.
\end{proof}

An equivalent formulation used repeatedly is the \emph{shared-mass identity}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shared}
\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x))=1-\dtv(p,q),
\end{equation}
which follows from $\min(a,b)=\tfrac12(a+b-|a-b|)$.

\subsection{Immediate corollaries}

\begin{corollary}[Two-sided form]\label{cor:twosided}
$|\Delta_{p,q}(A)|\le\dtv(p,q)$ for all $A$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Boolean distinguishers]
$\sup_f\bigl(\PR_p[f=1]-\PR_q[f=1]\bigr)=\dtv(p,q)$, attained by $f=\one_{A^\star}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Randomization does not help]\label{thm:soft}
For every $g:\X\to[0,1]$, $\bigl|\sum_x p(x)g(x)-\sum_x q(x)g(x)\bigr|\le\dtv(p,q)$, attained at $g=\one_{A^\star}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The soft advantage is linear in $g$ on the cube $[0,1]^{\X}$, whose extreme points are Boolean tests; alternatively bound directly by $\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))_+g(x)\le\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))_+$. Either route lands on Theorem~\ref{thm:eventsup}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp oscillation bound]\label{thm:osc}
If $m\le g(x)\le M$ for all $x$, then $|\E_p[g]-\E_q[g]|\le(M-m)\dtv(p,q)$, and the constant is sharp: with $m=0$, $M=1$, $g=\one_{A^\star}$, equality holds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Since $\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))=0$, recentre: $\E_p[g]-\E_q[g]=\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))(g(x)-m)$. Write $g-m=(M-m)h$ with $h:\X\to[0,1]$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:soft}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Strict lossiness of the $\ell^1$ estimate]
If $p\neq q$ then $\dtv(p,q)<\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|=2\dtv(p,q)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Range and rigid endpoints]\label{prop:range}
For laws $p,q$: (i) $0\le\dtv(p,q)\le1$; (ii) $\dtv(p,q)=0$ iff $p=q$; (iii) $\dtv(p,q)=1$ iff $p,q$ are mutually singular, i.e.\ $p(x)=0$ or $q(x)=0$ for every $x$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
All three follow from \eqref{eq:shared}: $\sum_x\min(p,q)=1-\dtv$ is a sum of non-negative terms bounded by $1$; it vanishes exactly under mutual singularity; and $\dtv=0$ iff $\sum_x|p-q|=0$.
\end{proof}

\section{Where the factor of two lives}

\begin{definition}[Signed advantage]
$\adv^{\pm}_{p,q}(g)=\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))g(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[$\ell^\infty$-dual description of the $\ell^1$ norm]
$\max_{\|g\|_\infty\le1}\adv^{\pm}_{p,q}(g)=\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|=2\dtv(p,q)$, attained at $g=\sgn(p-q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Termwise, $(p(x)-q(x))g(x)\le|p(x)-q(x)||g(x)|\le|p(x)-q(x)|$; the sign pattern realizes equality everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Factor-two dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
For laws $p,q$,
\[
\max_{g:\X\to[0,1]}\adv^{\pm}_{p,q}(g)=\dtv(p,q),\qquad
\max_{g:\X\to[-1,1]}\adv^{\pm}_{p,q}(g)=2\dtv(p,q),
\]
attained at $\one_{A^\star}$ and $\sgn(p-q)$ respectively.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[The invisible affine shift]\label{lem:shift}
For laws $p,q$ and any $g:\X\to\mathbb{R}$,
$\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))\frac{1+g(x)}{2}=\frac12\adv^{\pm}_{p,q}(g)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand; the constant term contributes $\tfrac12\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))=0$.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:shift} is the precise content of the ``factor of two''. The affine bijection $g\mapsto(1+g)/2$ carries $[-1,1]^{\X}$ onto $[0,1]^{\X}$; mass conservation annihilates the shift; the scaling by $\tfrac12$ survives. Neither optimum is ``the right one'' in the abstract: $[0,1]$-tests are the probabilistic ones, so their optimum is a probability, while $[-1,1]$ is the unit ball of $\ell^\infty$, so its optimum is the dual norm.

\begin{proposition}[Metric properties]
$\dtv$ is symmetric, vanishes exactly on the diagonal, and satisfies the triangle inequality.
\end{proposition}

\section{The coupling characterization}

\begin{definition}[Coupling]
$c:\X\times\X\to\mathbb{R}$ is a \emph{coupling} of $p$ and $q$ if $c\ge0$, $\sum_y c(x,y)=p(x)$ for all $x$, and $\sum_x c(x,y)=q(y)$ for all $y$. Write $c\in\Pi(p,q)$; this transport polytope is nonempty, containing $p\otimes q$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Disagreement probability]
$\PR_c[X\neq Y]=\sum_x\sum_{y\neq x}c(x,y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Diagonal form]\label{lem:diag}
If $c\in\Pi(p,q)$ then $\PR_c[X\neq Y]=1-\sum_x c(x,x)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For fixed $x$, $\sum_{y\neq x}c(x,y)=p(x)-c(x,x)$; sum over $x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Coupling bound on distinguishing gaps]\label{thm:cplgap}
Let $c\in\Pi(p,q)$ and $A\subseteq\X$. Then $p(A)-q(A)\le\PR_c[X\neq Y]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By the marginal conditions, $p(A)=\sum_{x,y}c(x,y)\one_A(x)$ and $q(A)=\sum_{x,y}c(x,y)\one_A(y)$, so
$p(A)-q(A)=\sum_{x,y}c(x,y)(\one_A(x)-\one_A(y))$. The bracket vanishes on the diagonal and is at most $1$ elsewhere, and $c\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Coupling lower bound]\label{cor:cpllower}
For every $c\in\Pi(p,q)$, $\dtv(p,q)\le\PR_c[X\neq Y]$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take $A=A^\star$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:cplgap} and apply the attainment half of Theorem~\ref{thm:eventsup}.
\end{proof}

Corollary~\ref{cor:cpllower} makes the duality explicit: the certificate that no coupling beats $\dtv$ is the optimal \emph{event}.

Let $t=\dtv(p,q)$, $m(x)=\min(p(x),q(x))$, so $\sum_x m(x)=1-t$ by \eqref{eq:shared}. Define the leftovers $p^\sharp=p-m$ and $q^\sharp=q-m$; both are non-negative, both sum to $t$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:disjoint}
p^\sharp(x)q^\sharp(x)=0\quad\text{for every }x,
\end{equation}
since at each point the minimum is attained by one of the two.

\begin{definition}[Maximal coupling]
\[
c^\star(x,y)=m(x)\one[x=y]+\begin{cases}\dfrac{p^\sharp(x)q^\sharp(y)}{t}, & t>0,\\[4pt] 0,& t=0.\end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Maximal coupling is a coupling]\label{thm:iscpl}
$c^\star\in\Pi(p,q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Non-negativity is clear. For $t>0$, $\sum_y c^\star(x,y)=m(x)+\frac{p^\sharp(x)}{t}\sum_y q^\sharp(y)=m(x)+p^\sharp(x)=p(x)$; the other marginal is symmetric. For $t=0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:range}(ii) gives $p=q$ and $c^\star$ is the diagonal coupling.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The maximal coupling attains $\dtv$]\label{thm:cplattain}
$\PR_{c^\star}[X\neq Y]=\dtv(p,q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $t>0$, $\sum_x c^\star(x,x)=\sum_x m(x)+\frac1t\sum_x p^\sharp(x)q^\sharp(x)=(1-t)+0=1-t$ by \eqref{eq:disjoint}; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:diag}. For $t=0$ the diagonal coupling never disagrees.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Coupling characterization]\label{thm:strassen}
$\dtv(p,q)=\min_{c\in\Pi(p,q)}\PR_c[X\neq Y]$, attained at $c^\star$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Minimax identity with explicit witnesses]
\[
\max_{A\subseteq\X}\bigl(p(A)-q(A)\bigr)=\dtv(p,q)=\min_{c\in\Pi(p,q)}\PR_c[X\neq Y],
\]
the maximum attained at $A^\star=\{q\le p\}$ and the minimum at $c^\star$.
\end{theorem}

Under the $\ell^1$ normalization this identity is not merely uglier but type-incorrect: the middle term would be $\|p-q\|_1$, which can reach $2$, while the right-hand side is a probability.

\section{Hypothesis testing and data processing}

\begin{definition}[Average error]
For $f:\X\to\{0,1\}$ declaring ``$q$'' when $f(x)=1$,
$\err_{p,q}(f)=\tfrac12\bigl(p(f^{-1}(1))+q(f^{-1}(0))\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Error is affine in the gap]\label{lem:affine}
With $A=f^{-1}(1)$, $\err_{p,q}(f)=\tfrac12\bigl(1+(p(A)-q(A))\bigr)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Le Cam two-point bound, exact form]\label{thm:lecam}
$\min_f\err_{p,q}(f)=\dfrac{1-\dtv(p,q)}{2}$, attained by $f=\one_{\{p\le q\}}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:affine}, minimizing the error means maximizing $q(A)-p(A)$, whose maximum is $\dtv(q,p)=\dtv(p,q)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:eventsup}.
\end{proof}

The $\ell^1$-normalized surrogate $\tfrac12(1-\|p-q\|_1)$ is negative --- hence vacuous --- as soon as the two laws are more than half apart, precisely the interesting regime.

\begin{definition}[Stochastic channel]
$K:\X\times\Y\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ with $\sum_y K(x,y)=1$; its action is $(pK)(y)=\sum_x p(x)K(x,y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Data-processing inequality]\label{thm:dpi}
For every channel $K$, $\dtv(pK,qK)\le\dtv(p,q)$. In particular $\dtv(T_*p,T_*q)\le\dtv(p,q)$ for any deterministic map $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\sum_y|\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))K(x,y)|\le\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|\sum_yK(x,y)=\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|$; halve.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Product law]
$p^{\otimes n}(v)=\prod_{i=1}^n p(v_i)$ for $v\in\X^n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Hybrid bound]\label{thm:hybrid}
$\dtv(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})\le n\,\dtv(p,q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction, using $\dtv(p_1\otimes p_2,q_1\otimes q_2)\le\dtv(p_1,q_1)+\dtv(p_2,q_2)$, itself proved by inserting the hybrid $p_1\otimes q_2$ and applying the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

\section{Sharp $n$-sample amplification}

\begin{definition}[Product coupling]
For $c\in\Pi(p,q)$, $c^{\otimes n}(v,w)=\prod_{i=1}^n c(v_i,w_i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:powcpl}
If $c\in\Pi(p,q)$ then $c^{\otimes n}\in\Pi(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\sum_w\prod_i c(v_i,w_i)=\prod_i\sum_{w_i}c(v_i,w_i)=\prod_i p(v_i)$, i.e.\ distributivity of a product of sums over the product index set.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Agreement tensorizes exactly]\label{lem:diagpow}
$\sum_v c^{\otimes n}(v,v)=\bigl(\sum_x c(x,x)\bigr)^n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Geometric amplification law]\label{thm:amp}
For laws $p,q$ and every $n$,
\[
\dtv\bigl(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n}\bigr)\le 1-\bigl(1-\dtv(p,q)\bigr)^n.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:powcpl} to $c^\star$. Its diagonal mass is $(1-\dtv(p,q))^n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:diagpow} and Theorem~\ref{thm:cplattain}, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:diag} its disagreement probability is $1-(1-\dtv)^n$; conclude with Corollary~\ref{cor:cpllower} applied to the product laws.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The geometric law dominates the linear one]\label{prop:dominates}
For $t\in[0,1]$ and all $n$, $1-(1-t)^n\le nt$; for $0<t<1$ and $n\ge2$ the inequality is strict.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction: $1-(1-t)^{n+1}=t+(1-t)(1-(1-t)^n)\le t+(1-t)nt\le t+nt$, with strictness entering once $t(1-t)>0$ and $n\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp sample-complexity floor]\label{cor:floor}
For every test $f:\X^n\to\{0,1\}$,
$\err_{p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n}}(f)\ge\tfrac12\bigl(1-\dtv(p,q)\bigr)^n$.
\end{corollary}

This is never vacuous, degrades exponentially rather than falling off a cliff, and exhibits the correct scaling $n=\Theta(1/\dtv)$ since $(1-t)^n\approx e^{-nt}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:amp} is \emph{not} attained in general: the exact $n$-sample distance lies strictly below $1-(1-\dtv)^n$ whenever $0<\dtv<1$ and $n\ge2$, because the product of maximal couplings need not itself be maximal.

\section{From divergence control to event control}

Let $\KL(Q\Vert P)=\sum_x Q(x)\log\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}$, assuming $P(x)=0\Rightarrow Q(x)=0$. Pinsker's inequality in the sharp normalization reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pinsker}
\dtv(Q,P)^2\le\tfrac12\KL(Q\Vert P),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \dtv(Q,P)\le\sqrt{\KL(Q\Vert P)/2}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Event-wise and test-wise Pinsker]
For every event $A$ and every $g:\X\to[0,1]$,
\[
|Q(A)-P(A)|\le\sqrt{\tfrac12\KL(Q\Vert P)},\qquad |\E_Q[g]-\E_P[g]|\le\sqrt{\tfrac12\KL(Q\Vert P)}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Converse certificate]
For every event $A$, $\KL(Q\Vert P)\ge2(Q(A)-P(A))^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Square Corollary~\ref{cor:twosided} and insert into \eqref{eq:pinsker}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[KL-driven testing bounds]
Every Boolean test satisfies $\err_{Q,P}(f)\ge\tfrac12\bigl(1-\sqrt{\KL(Q\Vert P)/2}\bigr)$, and after $n$ i.i.d.\ samples every test $f:\X^n\to\{0,1\}$ satisfies $\err_{Q^{\otimes n},P^{\otimes n}}(f)\ge\tfrac12\bigl(1-n\sqrt{\KL(Q\Vert P)/2}\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[KL-driven coupling]
There exists a coupling $c$ of $Q$ and $P$ with $\PR_c[X\neq Y]\le\sqrt{\KL(Q\Vert P)/2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
Under the $\ell^1$ convention Pinsker reads $\|Q-P\|_1\le\sqrt{2\KL}$, and the derived error bound $(1-\sqrt{2\KL})/2$ is non-positive as soon as $\KL\ge\tfrac12$; the sharp version stays informative until $\KL=2$. On $\KL\in[\tfrac18,\tfrac12]$ the lossy version is vacuous while the sharp one certifies a strictly positive error floor.
\end{remark}

\section{The Shtarkov sum is the multi-hypothesis testing optimum}

Let $\{p_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a family of $m=|\Theta|$ laws on $\X$.

\begin{definition}[Shtarkov sum]
$C_S=\sum_{x\in\X}\max_{\theta\in\Theta}p_\theta(x)$. In universal coding, $\log_2 C_S$ is the minimax regret.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Uniform-prior $m$-ary error]
For $T:\X\to\Theta$, $\err(T)=\frac1m\sum_\theta\sum_{x:T(x)\neq\theta}p_\theta(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Multi-hypothesis optimum]\label{thm:mary}
$\min_T\err(T)=1-\dfrac{C_S}{m}$, attained by the maximum-likelihood rule $T_{\mathrm{ML}}(x)\in\arg\max_\theta p_\theta(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Since $\sum_x p_\theta(x)=1$,
$\err(T)=\frac1m\sum_\theta\bigl(1-\sum_{x:T(x)=\theta}p_\theta(x)\bigr)=1-\frac1m\sum_x p_{T(x)}(x)$,
and $\sum_x p_{T(x)}(x)$ is maximized pointwise at a maximizer of $\theta\mapsto p_\theta(x)$, giving $C_S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Binary consistency]
For $m=2$ with sources $p,q$: $\max(a,b)=\min(a,b)+|a-b|$ gives $C_S=(1-\dtv)+2\dtv=1+\dtv(p,q)$, hence $\min_T\err(T)=\frac{1-\dtv(p,q)}{2}$, recovering Theorem~\ref{thm:lecam} exactly.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Rigid endpoints]
$\min_T\err(T)=0$ iff $C_S=m$ iff the sources are mutually singular. If all sources coincide, $C_S=1$ and the optimum is $1-1/m$: pure guessing.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Multi-hypothesis Le Cam bound]
If $\dtv(p_\theta,p_{\theta_0})\le\varepsilon/m$ for all $\theta$, then every rule satisfies $\err(T)\ge1-\frac1m-\frac{\varepsilon}{m}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Replace each $p_\theta$ by $p_{\theta_0}$ inside the fibre sums, paying $\dtv(p_\theta,p_{\theta_0})$ per hypothesis by Corollary~\ref{cor:twosided} applied to the fibre $T^{-1}(\theta)$. The reference terms sum to $1/m$ and the errors to at most $\varepsilon/m$.
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithmic content}

Every optimum above is computable in near-linear time in $N=|\X|$, a direct consequence of having explicit witnesses.

\begin{algorithmbox}[Distance and optimal event]
Compute $t\leftarrow\tfrac12\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|$ and $A^\star\leftarrow\{x:q(x)\le p(x)\}$ in a single pass: $\Theta(N)$ time, $\Theta(1)$ extra space. The optimal Boolean test and the optimal error $(1-t)/2$ follow immediately.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Maximal coupling]
Compute $m=\min(p,q)$, $p^\sharp=p-m$, $q^\sharp=q-m$, $t=\sum_x p^\sharp(x)$; return the sparse representation consisting of the diagonal weights $m(x)$ plus, if $t>0$, the rank-one block $p^\sharp\otimes q^\sharp/t$ on $\supp(p^\sharp)\times\supp(q^\sharp)$. Sampling costs $\Theta(\log N)$ after $\Theta(N)$ preprocessing: with probability $1-t$ draw $x\sim m/(1-t)$ and output $(x,x)$; otherwise draw $X\sim p^\sharp/t$ and $Y\sim q^\sharp/t$ independently.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Exact $n$-sample distance versus the two bounds]
For small $N,n$, enumerate $\X^n$, form the product laws, and compare the exact distance with $1-(1-t)^n$ and $nt$. Cost $\Theta(N^n)$; aggregating over multinomial type classes reduces this to $\Theta\bigl(\binom{n+N-1}{N-1}\bigr)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Multi-hypothesis optimum]
Compute $C_S=\sum_x\max_\theta p_\theta(x)$ and the maximum-likelihood rule in $\Theta(mN)$ time; the optimum is $1-C_S/m$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Applications}

\textbf{Learning-theoretic lower bounds.} The two-point method requires an exact relation between distance and error; Theorem~\ref{thm:lecam} supplies it, and Corollary~\ref{cor:floor} supplies the $n$-sample version with exponential rather than vacuous decay.

\textbf{Distribution shift.} Theorem~\ref{thm:osc} says that if deployment data sits within $\varepsilon$ of training data in total variation, every $[0,1]$-valued metric shifts by at most $\varepsilon$, and this worst case is attained.

\textbf{Privacy and indistinguishability.} ``No adversary distinguishes the two worlds with advantage more than $\varepsilon$'' is \emph{equivalent} to $\dtv\le\varepsilon$, quantifying over deterministic and randomized adversaries alike; Theorem~\ref{thm:dpi} yields post-processing invariance and Theorem~\ref{thm:amp} the exact degradation under repeated releases.

\textbf{Simulation and Markov chains.} The maximal coupling underlies coupling proofs of mixing; Theorem~\ref{thm:strassen} is the reason the method is not lossy in principle.

\textbf{Generative model evaluation.} A divergence estimate bounds the best possible discriminator, and an observed discriminator gap certifies a divergence lower bound.

\textbf{Universal compression.} The compression price satisfies $C_S/m=1-\min_T\err(T)$: minimax regret is $m$ times the identifiability of the family.

\section{Discussion and future directions}\label{sec:disc}

\subsection{Residual gaps}

Three gaps organize the future work. (1) The minimax identity was proved constructively, by exhibiting both optima, not by duality; the underlying finite-dimensional minimax theorem is not yet part of the development. (2) Geometric amplification is not tight: the exact $\dtv(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})$ lies strictly below $1-(1-\dtv)^n$ whenever $0<\dtv<1$. (3) Pinsker is the only divergence bridge present; $\sqrt{\KL/2}$ is lossy near $\KL\approx1$, whereas Bretagnolle--Huber, $\dtv\le\sqrt{1-e^{-\KL}}$, is not.

\subsection{Conjecture: exact Hellinger amplification law}

\begin{conjecture}
With the Hellinger affinity $\rho(p,q)=\sum_x\sqrt{p(x)q(x)}$, for finite laws $p,q$,
\[
1-\rho(p,q)^n\le\dtv\bigl(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n}\bigr)\le\sqrt{1-\rho(p,q)^{2n}},
\]
and both bounds are strictly sharper than $1-(1-\dtv(p,q))^n$ whenever $0<\dtv(p,q)<1$.
\end{conjecture}

The affinity, unlike total variation, is exactly multiplicative over products, $\rho(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})=\rho(p,q)^n$, so it is the natural carrier of tensorization while $\dtv$ is the natural carrier of testing; the two are linked by the Le Cam sandwich $1-\rho\le\dtv\le\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$. Structurally, the shared-mass functional $\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x))=1-\dtv$ becomes the affinity when $\min$ is replaced by the geometric mean, and multiplicativity reuses the same product-of-sums interchange as Lemma~\ref{lem:diagpow}.

\subsection{Conjecture: a duality proof of the minimax identity}

\begin{conjecture}
The identity $\max_A(p(A)-q(A))=\min_{c\in\Pi(p,q)}\PR_c[X\neq Y]$ is an instance of finite linear-programming duality, and equality can be established without constructing the maximal coupling: the vertices of the transport polytope are the extreme couplings, and complementary slackness identifies the likelihood-ratio event as the active constraint.
\end{conjecture}

The maximal coupling would then be not a lucky formula but the unique dual optimum whose support is forced by complementary slackness against the indicator of $\{q\le p\}$: the diagonal is where the primal constraint is tight, and the rank-one leftover block is exactly the residual flow the slack constraints permit.

\subsection{Further directions}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Bretagnolle--Huber bridge.} Add $\dtv\le\sqrt{1-e^{-\KL}}$ alongside Pinsker; it dominates $\sqrt{\KL/2}$ for large divergence and never goes vacuous.
\item \textbf{Exact product distance.} Characterize $\dtv(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})$ via multinomial type classes, whose asymptotics are governed by a Chernoff exponent, quantifying exactly how much Theorem~\ref{thm:amp} loses.
\item \textbf{Beyond uniform priors.} For a general prior $\pi$ the optimum becomes $1-\sum_x\max_\theta\pi(\theta)p_\theta(x)$, a weighted Shtarkov sum.
\item \textbf{Continuous state spaces.} The constructive route --- explicit optimal event, explicit maximal coupling from the Lebesgue decomposition --- carries over and would make the general statement equally witness-bearing.
\item \textbf{Approximate couplings.} Relaxing the marginal constraints yields interpolating distances whose testing interpretation quantifies $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-indistinguishability.
\end{itemize}

  "demo": """"
Sharper normalization: numerical demonstrations of the attained factor-1/2
theory of total variation distance.

Everything in this file is self-contained (standard library only) and verifies,
on concrete finite distributions, the results of the accompanying paper:

  1. Event-supremum characterization
         d_TV(p, q) = max_A ( p(A) - q(A) ),   attained at A* = {x : q(x) <= p(x)}
     checked against brute-force enumeration of all 2^N events.

  2. Randomization does not help: random [0,1]-valued tests never beat A*.

  3. Factor-two dichotomy: sup over [0,1]-tests is d_TV, sup over [-1,1]-tests
     is 2 d_TV = ||p - q||_1.

  4. Maximal coupling: c*(x,y) = min(p,q)(x)[x=y] + p#(x) q#(y) / d_TV
     is a coupling with P[X != Y] = d_TV exactly, and no coupling does better
     (checked against random couplings and against the independent coupling).

  5. Two-point testing: the least average error over all 2^N Boolean tests
     equals (1 - d_TV)/2.

  6. Data processing: random stochastic channels never increase d_TV.

  7. n-sample amplification: exact d_TV(p^n, q^n) versus the geometric bound
     1 - (1 - d_TV)^n and the hybrid bound n * d_TV.

  8. Pinsker bridge: d_TV <= sqrt(KL/2), and the converse certificate
     KL >= 2 * gap^2 for every event.

  9. Shtarkov sum = multi-hypothesis testing optimum: the least uniform-prior
     error of an m-ary rule equals 1 - C_S / m, checked by brute force over all
     m^N decision rules, with the binary case reproducing (1 - d_TV)/2.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, Sequence

Vec = Sequence[float]
Mat = Sequence[Sequence[float]]

TOL = 1e-9


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core quantities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def tv_distance(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """d_TV(p, q) = (1/2) * sum_x |p(x) - q(x)| -- the sharp normalization."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def l1_distance(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """||p - q||_1 = 2 * d_TV(p, q) -- the coarse normalization."""
    return sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def event_gap(p: Vec, q: Vec, event: Iterable[int]) -> float:
    """p(A) - q(A) for an event A given as a collection of indices."""
    idx = list(event)
    return sum(p[i] for i in idx) - sum(q[i] for i in idx)


def separating_event(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[int]:
    """The likelihood-ratio (Neyman-Pearson) event A* = {x : q(x) <= p(x)}."""
    return [i for i in range(len(p)) if q[i] <= p[i]]


def shared_mass(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """sum_x min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 - d_TV(p, q)."""
    return sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def all_events(n: int) -> Iterable[tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Enumerate every subset of {0, ..., n-1} as a tuple of indices."""
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        yield tuple(i for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1)


def brute_force_max_gap(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> tuple[float, tuple[int, ...]]:
    """max_A (p(A) - q(A)) by enumerating all 2^N events."""
    best_value = -math.inf
    best_event: tuple[int, ...] = ()
    for event in all_events(len(p)):
        value = event_gap(p, q, event)
        if value > best_value:
            best_value, best_event = value, event
    return best_value, best_event


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Couplings
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def maximal_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[list[float]]:
    """The maximal coupling: shared mass on the diagonal, leftovers paired
    independently and rescaled by t = d_TV(p, q)."""
    n = len(p)
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    m = [min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q)]
    p_sharp = [p[i] - m[i] for i in range(n)]
    q_sharp = [q[i] - m[i] for i in range(n)]
    c = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for x in range(n):
        c[x][x] += m[x]
    if t > TOL:
        for x in range(n):
            if p_sharp[x] == 0.0:
                continue
            for y in range(n):
                c[x][y] += p_sharp[x] * q_sharp[y] / t
    return c


def independent_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[list[float]]:
    """The product coupling c(x, y) = p(x) q(y)."""
    return [[a * b for b in q] for a in p]


def is_coupling(c: Mat, p: Vec, q: Vec) -> bool:
    """Check nonnegativity and both marginal constraints."""
    n = len(p)
    if any(c[x][y] < -TOL for x in range(n) for y in range(n)):
        return False
    if any(abs(sum(c[x]) - p[x]) > 1e-8 for x in range(n)):
        return False
    if any(abs(sum(c[x][y] for x in range(n)) - q[y]) > 1e-8 for y in range(n)):
        return False
    return True


def disagreement_probability(c: Mat) -> float:
    """P_c[X != Y] = sum over off-diagonal entries."""
    n = len(c)
    return sum(c[x][y] for x in range(n) for y in range(n) if x != y)


def random_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random, steps: int = 400) -> list[list[float]]:
    """A random point of the transport polytope, produced by starting at the
    independent coupling and applying random mass-preserving 2x2 rotations."""
    n = len(p)
    c = [row[:] for row in independent_coupling(p, q)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        x1, x2 = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
        y1, y2 = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
        if x1 == x2 or y1 == y2:
            continue
        delta = min(c[x1][y1], c[x2][y2]) * rng.random()
        c[x1][y1] -= delta
        c[x2][y2] -= delta
        c[x1][y2] += delta
        c[x2][y1] += delta
    return c


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Testing
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def bayes_error(p: Vec, q: Vec, accept_q: Iterable[int]) -> float:
    """Uniform-prior average error of the Boolean test that declares 'q'
    exactly on the index set accept_q."""
    a = set(accept_q)
    err_under_p = sum(p[i] for i in a)
    err_under_q = sum(q[i] for i in range(len(q)) if i not in a)
    return 0.5 * (err_under_p + err_under_q)


def brute_force_min_bayes_error(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """Least uniform-prior average error over all 2^N Boolean tests."""
    return min(bayes_error(p, q, event) for event in all_events(len(p)))


def shtarkov_sum(sources: Mat) -> float:
    """C_S = sum_x max_theta p_theta(x)."""
    n = len(sources[0])
    return sum(max(src[x] for src in sources) for x in range(n))


def m_ary_error(sources: Mat, rule: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Uniform-prior error of the decision rule x -> rule[x]."""
    m, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    total = 0.0
    for theta in range(m):
        total += sum(sources[theta][x] for x in range(n) if rule[x] != theta)
    return total / m


def brute_force_min_m_ary_error(sources: Mat) -> float:
    """Least uniform-prior error over all m^N decision rules."""
    m, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    return min(m_ary_error(sources, rule) for rule in itertools.product(range(m), repeat=n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Products, channels, divergence
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def product_law(p: Vec, n: int) -> list[float]:
    """p^{tensor n} as a flat vector over X^n in lexicographic order."""
    out = [1.0]
    for _ in range(n):
        out = [w * pi for w in out for pi in p]
    return out


def push_forward(p: Vec, kernel: Mat) -> list[float]:
    """(pK)(y) = sum_x p(x) K(x, y)."""
    n_out = len(kernel[0])
    return [sum(p[x] * kernel[x][y] for x in range(len(p))) for y in range(n_out)]


def random_channel(n_in: int, n_out: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[list[float]]:
    """A random row-stochastic matrix."""
    rows = []
    for _ in range(n_in):
        row = [rng.random() + 1e-3 for _ in range(n_out)]
        s = sum(row)
        rows.append([v / s for v in row])
    return rows


def kl_divergence(qq: Vec, pp: Vec) -> float:
    """KL(Q || P) in nats, with the convention 0 log 0 = 0."""
    total = 0.0
    for a, b in zip(qq, pp):
        if a > 0.0:
            if b <= 0.0:
                return math.inf
            total += a * math.log(a / b)
    return total


def random_law(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[float]:
    raw = [rng.random() + 1e-3 for _ in range(n)]
    s = sum(raw)
    return [v / s for v in raw]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def demo_event_supremum(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> None:
    banner("1. Event supremum:  d_TV = max_A (p(A) - q(A)), attained at {q <= p}")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    best_value, best_event = brute_force_max_gap(p, q)
    star = separating_event(p, q)
    print(f"p                       = {[round(v, 4) for v in p]}")
    print(f"q                       = {[round(v, 4) for v in q]}")
    print(f"d_TV(p, q)              = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"||p - q||_1             = {l1_distance(p, q):.10f}   (= 2 d_TV, strictly lossy)")
    print(f"max over all 2^N events = {best_value:.10f}   attained at A = {best_event}")
    print(f"likelihood-ratio event  = {tuple(star)}, gap = {event_gap(p, q, star):.10f}")
    print(f"shared mass sum min(p,q)= {shared_mass(p, q):.10f}   (= 1 - d_TV)")
    assert abs(best_value - t) < 1e-9
    assert abs(event_gap(p, q, star) - t) < 1e-9
    assert abs(shared_mass(p, q) - (1 - t)) < 1e-9
    print("OK: the supremum is attained and equals the sharp distance.")


def demo_randomized_tests(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("2-3. Randomization does not help; the factor-two dichotomy")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    n = len(p)
    best_soft = -math.inf
    best_signed = -math.inf
    for _ in range(200_000):
        g = [rng.random() for _ in range(n)]
        best_soft = max(best_soft, sum((p[i] - q[i]) * g[i] for i in range(n)))
        h = [2 * rng.random() - 1 for _ in range(n)]
        best_signed = max(best_signed, sum((p[i] - q[i]) * h[i] for i in range(n)))
    sign_test = [math.copysign(1.0, p[i] - q[i]) for i in range(n)]
    print(f"best random [0,1]-test advantage  = {best_soft:.6f}   <= d_TV      = {t:.6f}")
    print(f"best random [-1,1]-test advantage = {best_signed:.6f}   <= 2 d_TV    = {2 * t:.6f}")
    print(f"sign pattern sgn(p - q) advantage = "
          f"{sum((p[i] - q[i]) * sign_test[i] for i in range(n)):.10f}   (= 2 d_TV exactly)")
    assert best_soft <= t + 1e-9
    assert best_signed <= 2 * t + 1e-9
    assert abs(sum((p[i] - q[i]) * sign_test[i] for i in range(n)) - 2 * t) < 1e-9
    print("OK: [0,1]-tests cap at d_TV; [-1,1]-tests cap at 2 d_TV, attained at the sign pattern.")


def demo_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("4. Maximal coupling:  min over couplings of P[X != Y] = d_TV")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    c_star = maximal_coupling(p, q)
    c_ind = independent_coupling(p, q)
    print(f"maximal coupling is a valid coupling : {is_coupling(c_star, p, q)}")
    print(f"P_c*[X != Y]                         = {disagreement_probability(c_star):.10f}")
    print(f"d_TV(p, q)                           = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"independent coupling P[X != Y]       = {disagreement_probability(c_ind):.10f}")
    assert is_coupling(c_star, p, q)
    assert abs(disagreement_probability(c_star) - t) < 1e-9
    worst = math.inf
    for _ in range(2_000):
        c = random_coupling(p, q, rng)
        assert is_coupling(c, p, q)
        worst = min(worst, disagreement_probability(c))
    print(f"best of 2000 random couplings        = {worst:.10f}   >= d_TV")
    assert worst >= t - 1e-9
    print("OK: no coupling beats d_TV, and the explicit maximal coupling attains it.")


def demo_testing(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> None:
    banner("5. Two-point testing:  min error = (1 - d_TV)/2")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    best = brute_force_min_bayes_error(p, q)
    print(f"least error over all 2^N tests = {best:.10f}")
    print(f"(1 - d_TV)/2                   = {(1 - t) / 2:.10f}")
    print(f"lossy surrogate (1 - ||p-q||_1)/2 = {(1 - l1_distance(p, q)) / 2:+.10f}"
          f"{'   <-- VACUOUS (negative)' if 1 - l1_distance(p, q) < 0 else ''}")
    assert abs(best - (1 - t) / 2) < 1e-9
    print("OK: the sharp normalization gives the exact optimum; the lossy one can go negative.")


def demo_data_processing(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("6. Data processing: channels never increase d_TV")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    worst_ratio = 0.0
    for _ in range(5_000):
        k = random_channel(len(p), 3, rng)
        after = tv_distance(push_forward(p, k), push_forward(q, k))
        assert after <= t + 1e-9
        worst_ratio = max(worst_ratio, after / t if t > 0 else 0.0)
    print(f"d_TV(p, q)                                  = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"largest d_TV after 5000 random channels     = {worst_ratio * t:.10f}")
    print(f"largest ratio d_TV(pK, qK) / d_TV(p, q)     = {worst_ratio:.10f}   (<= 1)")
    print("OK: post-processing can only destroy distinguishability, never create it.")


def demo_amplification(p: Vec, q: Vec, max_n: int = 6) -> None:
    banner("7. n-sample amplification: exact vs geometric vs hybrid bound")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    print(f"single-sample d_TV = {t:.6f}")
    print()
    print(f"{'n':>2} | {'exact d_TV(p^n,q^n)':>20} | {'1-(1-d)^n':>12} | {'n*d':>10} | slack")
    print("-" * 74)
    for n in range(1, max_n + 1):
        exact = tv_distance(product_law(p, n), product_law(q, n))
        geometric = 1 - (1 - t) ** n
        hybrid = n * t
        assert exact <= geometric + 1e-9
        assert geometric <= hybrid + 1e-9
        print(f"{n:>2} | {exact:>20.10f} | {geometric:>12.8f} | {hybrid:>10.6f} |"
              f" {geometric - exact:.8f}")
    print()
    print("The geometric bound never exceeds 1; the hybrid bound goes vacuous once n >= 1/d_TV.")
    print("Residual slack (last column) is the gap that an exactly multiplicative")
    print("quantity such as the Hellinger affinity would be needed to close.")


def demo_pinsker(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 20_000) -> None:
    banner("8. Pinsker bridge: d_TV <= sqrt(KL/2), and KL >= 2 * gap^2")
    worst_slack = math.inf
    worst_pair = None
    for _ in range(trials):
        n = rng.choice([2, 3, 4])
        qq = random_law(n, rng)
        pp = random_law(n, rng)
        kl = kl_divergence(qq, pp)
        t = tv_distance(qq, pp)
        bound = math.sqrt(kl / 2)
        assert t <= bound + 1e-9
        for event in all_events(n):
            gap = event_gap(qq, pp, event)
            assert 2 * gap * gap <= kl + 1e-9
        if bound - t < worst_slack:
            worst_slack, worst_pair = bound - t, (qq, pp, t, kl)
    assert worst_pair is not None
    qq, pp, t, kl = worst_pair
    print(f"tightest instance found in {trials} random trials:")
    print(f"  Q            = {[round(v, 4) for v in qq]}")
    print(f"  P            = {[round(v, 4) for v in pp]}")
    print(f"  d_TV(Q, P)   = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"  sqrt(KL/2)   = {math.sqrt(kl / 2):.10f}")
    print(f"  KL(Q || P)   = {kl:.10f}   >=  2*d_TV^2 = {2 * t * t:.10f}")
    print()
    print("Where the normalization decides non-vacuity:")
    print(f"{'KL':>6} | {'sharp (1-sqrt(KL/2))/2':>24} | {'lossy (1-sqrt(2KL))/2':>24}")
    print("-" * 62)
    for kl_val in (0.05, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
        sharp = (1 - math.sqrt(kl_val / 2)) / 2
        lossy = (1 - math.sqrt(2 * kl_val)) / 2
        flag = "  <-- lossy vacuous" if lossy <= 0 < sharp else ""
        print(f"{kl_val:>6.3f} | {sharp:>24.6f} | {lossy:>24.6f}{flag}")
    print("OK: every event obeys the Pinsker bound and certifies a KL lower bound.")


def demo_multihypothesis(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("9. Shtarkov sum = multi-hypothesis optimum:  min error = 1 - C_S / m")
    for m, n in ((2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 3)):
        sources = [random_law(n, rng) for _ in range(m)]
        cs = shtarkov_sum(sources)
        predicted = 1 - cs / m
        actual = brute_force_min_m_ary_error(sources)
        ml_rule = [max(range(m), key=lambda th: sources[th][x]) for x in range(n)]
        ml_error = m_ary_error(sources, ml_rule)
        print(f"m = {m}, |X| = {n}:  C_S = {cs:.8f},  1 - C_S/m = {predicted:.10f},"
              f"  brute force = {actual:.10f},  ML rule = {ml_error:.10f}")
        assert abs(predicted - actual) < 1e-9
        assert abs(ml_error - actual) < 1e-9
    print()
    print("Binary consistency check (C_S = 1 + d_TV, so 1 - C_S/2 = (1 - d_TV)/2):")
    for _ in range(3):
        p, q = random_law(4, rng), random_law(4, rng)
        cs = shtarkov_sum([p, q])
        t = tv_distance(p, q)
        print(f"  d_TV = {t:.8f},  C_S = {cs:.8f},  1 + d_TV = {1 + t:.8f},"
              f"  1 - C_S/2 = {1 - cs / 2:.8f},  (1 - d_TV)/2 = {(1 - t) / 2:.8f}")
        assert abs(cs - (1 + t)) < 1e-9
        assert abs((1 - cs / 2) - (1 - t) / 2) < 1e-9
    print("OK: the universal-coding price and the testing optimum are the same number.")


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(20260824)

    # A running example on a five-letter alphabet.
    p = [0.35, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.05]
    q = [0.10, 0.30, 0.10, 0.25, 0.25]

    demo_event_supremum(p, q)
    demo_randomized_tests(p, q, rng)
    demo_coupling(p, q, rng)
    demo_testing(p, q)
    demo_data_processing(p, q, rng)
    demo_amplification([0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6], max_n=8)
    demo_pinsker(rng, trials=4_000)
    demo_multihypothesis(rng)

    banner("A near-singular pair, where the lossy normalization fails outright")
    p2 = [0.98, 0.01, 0.01]
    q2 = [0.01, 0.98, 0.01]
    t2 = tv_distance(p2, q2)
    print(f"p = {p2},  q = {q2}")
    print(f"d_TV        = {t2:.6f}         -> optimal test error (1 - d_TV)/2 = {(1 - t2) / 2:.6f}")
    print(f"||p - q||_1 = {l1_distance(p2, q2):.6f}   -> lossy surrogate "
          f"(1 - ||p-q||_1)/2 = {(1 - l1_distance(p2, q2)) / 2:+.6f}  (meaningless)")
    print(f"maximal coupling agrees with probability {1 - t2:.6f} = 1 - d_TV")
    print()
    print("All assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, Sequence

Vec = Sequence[float]
Mat = Sequence[Sequence[float]]

TOL = 1e-9


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core quantities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def tv_distance(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """d_TV(p, q) = (1/2) * sum_x |p(x) - q(x)| -- the sharp normalization."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def l1_distance(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """||p - q||_1 = 2 * d_TV(p, q) -- the coarse normalization."""
    return sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def event_gap(p: Vec, q: Vec, event: Iterable[int]) -> float:
    """p(A) - q(A) for an event A given as a collection of indices."""
    idx = list(event)
    return sum(p[i] for i in idx) - sum(q[i] for i in idx)


def separating_event(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[int]:
    """The likelihood-ratio (Neyman-Pearson) event A* = {x : q(x) <= p(x)}."""
    return [i for i in range(len(p)) if q[i] <= p[i]]


def shared_mass(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """sum_x min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 - d_TV(p, q)."""
    return sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def all_events(n: int) -> Iterable[tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Enumerate every subset of {0, ..., n-1} as a tuple of indices."""
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        yield tuple(i for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1)


def brute_force_max_gap(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> tuple[float, tuple[int, ...]]:
    """max_A (p(A) - q(A)) by enumerating all 2^N events."""
    best_value = -math.inf
    best_event: tuple[int, ...] = ()
    for event in all_events(len(p)):
        value = event_gap(p, q, event)
        if value > best_value:
            best_value, best_event = value, event
    return best_value, best_event


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Couplings
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def maximal_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[list[float]]:
    """The maximal coupling: shared mass on the diagonal, leftovers paired
    independently and rescaled by t = d_TV(p, q)."""
    n = len(p)
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    m = [min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q)]
    p_sharp = [p[i] - m[i] for i in range(n)]
    q_sharp = [q[i] - m[i] for i in range(n)]
    c = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for x in range(n):
        c[x][x] += m[x]
    if t > TOL:
        for x in range(n):
            if p_sharp[x] == 0.0:
                continue
            for y in range(n):
                c[x][y] += p_sharp[x] * q_sharp[y] / t
    return c


def independent_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[list[float]]:
    """The product coupling c(x, y) = p(x) q(y)."""
    return [[a * b for b in q] for a in p]


def is_coupling(c: Mat, p: Vec, q: Vec) -> bool:
    """Check nonnegativity and both marginal constraints."""
    n = len(p)
    if any(c[x][y] < -TOL for x in range(n) for y in range(n)):
        return False
    if any(abs(sum(c[x]) - p[x]) > 1e-8 for x in range(n)):
        return False
    if any(abs(sum(c[x][y] for x in range(n)) - q[y]) > 1e-8 for y in range(n)):
        return False
    return True


def disagreement_probability(c: Mat) -> float:
    """P_c[X != Y] = sum over off-diagonal entries."""
    n = len(c)
    return sum(c[x][y] for x in range(n) for y in range(n) if x != y)


def random_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random, steps: int = 400) -> list[list[float]]:
    """A random point of the transport polytope, produced by starting at the
    independent coupling and applying random mass-preserving 2x2 rotations."""
    n = len(p)
    c = [row[:] for row in independent_coupling(p, q)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        x1, x2 = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
        y1, y2 = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
        if x1 == x2 or y1 == y2:
            continue
        delta = min(c[x1][y1], c[x2][y2]) * rng.random()
        c[x1][y1] -= delta
        c[x2][y2] -= delta
        c[x1][y2] += delta
        c[x2][y1] += delta
    return c


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Testing
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def bayes_error(p: Vec, q: Vec, accept_q: Iterable[int]) -> float:
    """Uniform-prior average error of the Boolean test that declares 'q'
    exactly on the index set accept_q."""
    a = set(accept_q)
    err_under_p = sum(p[i] for i in a)
    err_under_q = sum(q[i] for i in range(len(q)) if i not in a)
    return 0.5 * (err_under_p + err_under_q)


def brute_force_min_bayes_error(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> float:
    """Least uniform-prior average error over all 2^N Boolean tests."""
    return min(bayes_error(p, q, event) for event in all_events(len(p)))


def shtarkov_sum(sources: Mat) -> float:
    """C_S = sum_x max_theta p_theta(x)."""
    n = len(sources[0])
    return sum(max(src[x] for src in sources) for x in range(n))


def m_ary_error(sources: Mat, rule: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Uniform-prior error of the decision rule x -> rule[x]."""
    m, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    total = 0.0
    for theta in range(m):
        total += sum(sources[theta][x] for x in range(n) if rule[x] != theta)
    return total / m


def brute_force_min_m_ary_error(sources: Mat) -> float:
    """Least uniform-prior error over all m^N decision rules."""
    m, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    return min(m_ary_error(sources, rule) for rule in itertools.product(range(m), repeat=n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Products, channels, divergence
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def product_law(p: Vec, n: int) -> list[float]:
    """p^{tensor n} as a flat vector over X^n in lexicographic order."""
    out = [1.0]
    for _ in range(n):
        out = [w * pi for w in out for pi in p]
    return out


def push_forward(p: Vec, kernel: Mat) -> list[float]:
    """(pK)(y) = sum_x p(x) K(x, y)."""
    n_out = len(kernel[0])
    return [sum(p[x] * kernel[x][y] for x in range(len(p))) for y in range(n_out)]


def random_channel(n_in: int, n_out: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[list[float]]:
    """A random row-stochastic matrix."""
    rows = []
    for _ in range(n_in):
        row = [rng.random() + 1e-3 for _ in range(n_out)]
        s = sum(row)
        rows.append([v / s for v in row])
    return rows


def kl_divergence(qq: Vec, pp: Vec) -> float:
    """KL(Q || P) in nats, with the convention 0 log 0 = 0."""
    total = 0.0
    for a, b in zip(qq, pp):
        if a > 0.0:
            if b <= 0.0:
                return math.inf
            total += a * math.log(a / b)
    return total


def random_law(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[float]:
    raw = [rng.random() + 1e-3 for _ in range(n)]
    s = sum(raw)
    return [v / s for v in raw]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def demo_event_supremum(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> None:
    banner("1. Event supremum:  d_TV = max_A (p(A) - q(A)), attained at {q <= p}")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    best_value, best_event = brute_force_max_gap(p, q)
    star = separating_event(p, q)
    print(f"p                       = {[round(v, 4) for v in p]}")
    print(f"q                       = {[round(v, 4) for v in q]}")
    print(f"d_TV(p, q)              = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"||p - q||_1             = {l1_distance(p, q):.10f}   (= 2 d_TV, strictly lossy)")
    print(f"max over all 2^N events = {best_value:.10f}   attained at A = {best_event}")
    print(f"likelihood-ratio event  = {tuple(star)}, gap = {event_gap(p, q, star):.10f}")
    print(f"shared mass sum min(p,q)= {shared_mass(p, q):.10f}   (= 1 - d_TV)")
    assert abs(best_value - t) < 1e-9
    assert abs(event_gap(p, q, star) - t) < 1e-9
    assert abs(shared_mass(p, q) - (1 - t)) < 1e-9
    print("OK: the supremum is attained and equals the sharp distance.")


def demo_randomized_tests(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("2-3. Randomization does not help; the factor-two dichotomy")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    n = len(p)
    best_soft = -math.inf
    best_signed = -math.inf
    for _ in range(200_000):
        g = [rng.random() for _ in range(n)]
        best_soft = max(best_soft, sum((p[i] - q[i]) * g[i] for i in range(n)))
        h = [2 * rng.random() - 1 for _ in range(n)]
        best_signed = max(best_signed, sum((p[i] - q[i]) * h[i] for i in range(n)))
    sign_test = [math.copysign(1.0, p[i] - q[i]) for i in range(n)]
    print(f"best random [0,1]-test advantage  = {best_soft:.6f}   <= d_TV      = {t:.6f}")
    print(f"best random [-1,1]-test advantage = {best_signed:.6f}   <= 2 d_TV    = {2 * t:.6f}")
    print(f"sign pattern sgn(p - q) advantage = "
          f"{sum((p[i] - q[i]) * sign_test[i] for i in range(n)):.10f}   (= 2 d_TV exactly)")
    assert best_soft <= t + 1e-9
    assert best_signed <= 2 * t + 1e-9
    assert abs(sum((p[i] - q[i]) * sign_test[i] for i in range(n)) - 2 * t) < 1e-9
    print("OK: [0,1]-tests cap at d_TV; [-1,1]-tests cap at 2 d_TV, attained at the sign pattern.")


def demo_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("4. Maximal coupling:  min over couplings of P[X != Y] = d_TV")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    c_star = maximal_coupling(p, q)
    c_ind = independent_coupling(p, q)
    print(f"maximal coupling is a valid coupling : {is_coupling(c_star, p, q)}")
    print(f"P_c*[X != Y]                         = {disagreement_probability(c_star):.10f}")
    print(f"d_TV(p, q)                           = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"independent coupling P[X != Y]       = {disagreement_probability(c_ind):.10f}")
    assert is_coupling(c_star, p, q)
    assert abs(disagreement_probability(c_star) - t) < 1e-9
    worst = math.inf
    for _ in range(2_000):
        c = random_coupling(p, q, rng)
        assert is_coupling(c, p, q)
        worst = min(worst, disagreement_probability(c))
    print(f"best of 2000 random couplings        = {worst:.10f}   >= d_TV")
    assert worst >= t - 1e-9
    print("OK: no coupling beats d_TV, and the explicit maximal coupling attains it.")


def demo_testing(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> None:
    banner("5. Two-point testing:  min error = (1 - d_TV)/2")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    best = brute_force_min_bayes_error(p, q)
    print(f"least error over all 2^N tests = {best:.10f}")
    print(f"(1 - d_TV)/2                   = {(1 - t) / 2:.10f}")
    print(f"lossy surrogate (1 - ||p-q||_1)/2 = {(1 - l1_distance(p, q)) / 2:+.10f}"
          f"{'   <-- VACUOUS (negative)' if 1 - l1_distance(p, q) < 0 else ''}")
    assert abs(best - (1 - t) / 2) < 1e-9
    print("OK: the sharp normalization gives the exact optimum; the lossy one can go negative.")


def demo_data_processing(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    banner("6. Data processing: channels never increase d_TV")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    worst_ratio = 0.0
    for _ in range(5_000):
        k = random_channel(len(p), 3, rng)
        after = tv_distance(push_forward(p, k), push_forward(q, k))
        assert after <= t + 1e-9
        worst_ratio = max(worst_ratio, after / t if t > 0 else 0.0)
    print(f"d_TV(p, q)                                  = {t:.10f}")
    print(f"largest d_TV after 5000 random channels     = {worst_ratio * t:.10f}")
    print(f"largest ratio d_TV(pK, qK) / d_TV(p, q)     = {worst_ratio:.10f}   (<= 1)")
    print("OK: post-processing can only destroy distinguishability, never create it.")


def demo_amplification(p: Vec, q: Vec, max_n: int = 6) -> None:
    banner("7. n-sample amplification: exact vs geometric vs hybrid bound")
    t = tv_distance(p, q)
    print(f"single-sample d_TV = {t:.6f}")
    print()
    print(f"{'n':>2} | {'exact d_TV(p^n,q^n)':>20} | {'1-(1-d)^n':>12} | {'n*d':>10} | slack")
    print("-" * 74)
    for n in range(1, max_n + 1):
        exact = tv_distance(product_law(p, n), product_law(q, n))
        geometric = 1 - (1 - t) ** n
        hybrid = n * t
        assert exact <= geometric + 1e-9
        assert geometric <= hybrid + 1e-9
        print(f"{n:>2} | {exact:>20.10f} | {geometric:>12.8f} | {hybrid:>10.6f} |"
              f" {geometric - exact:.8f}")
    print()
    print("The geometric bound never exceeds 1; the hybrid bound goes vacuous once n >= 1/d_TV.")
    print("Residual slack (last column) is the gap that an exactly multiplicative")
    print("quantity such as the Hellinger affinity would be needed to close.")

    for _ in range(trials):

        if bound - t < worst_slack:

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence

Vec = Sequence[float]


def optimal_event_certificate(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Return the sharp total variation distance together with the primal witness.

    The returned dictionary contains
      'd_tv'         : (1/2) * sum_x |p(x) - q(x)|,
      'event'        : the likelihood-ratio event A* = {x : q(x) <= p(x)},
      'gap'          : p(A*) - q(A*), which provably equals 'd_tv',
      'shared_mass'  : sum_x min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 - d_tv,
      'optimal_error': (1 - d_tv)/2, the least average error of any Boolean test,
      'l1'           : ||p - q||_1 = 2 * d_tv, the coarse normalization.
    Complexity: Theta(N) time and Theta(|A*|) space for N = len(p).
    """
    if len(p) != len(q):
        raise ValueError("distributions must share an alphabet")
    surplus = 0.0
    deficit = 0.0
    shared = 0.0
    event: list[int] = []
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(p, q)):
        diff = a - b
        if diff >= 0.0:
            surplus += diff
            event.append(i)
            shared += b
        else:
            deficit -= diff
            shared += a
    d_tv = 0.5 * (surplus + deficit)
    return {
        "d_tv": d_tv,
        "event": event,
        "gap": surplus,          # equals d_tv, since surplus == deficit
        "shared_mass": shared,   # equals 1 - d_tv
        "optimal_error": 0.5 * (1.0 - d_tv),
        "l1": 2.0 * d_tv,
    }


def optimal_boolean_test(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[int]:
    """The optimal distinguisher as a 0/1 vector: output 1 exactly on A*."""
    return [1 if q[i] <= p[i] else 0 for i in range(len(p))]

from __future__ import annotations

import bisect
import random
from typing import Sequence

Vec = Sequence[float]


def build_maximal_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Sparse representation of the coupling of p and q that agrees most often.

    Structure returned:
      'shared'    : m(x) = min(p(x), q(x)), the diagonal block (total 1 - d_tv),
      'p_leftover': p# = p - m       (total d_tv),
      'q_leftover': q# = q - m       (total d_tv),
      'd_tv'      : the total variation distance, which is also P[X != Y].
    The full joint law is
        c*(x, y) = m(x)*[x == y] + p#(x) q#(y) / d_tv     (the second term absent
    when d_tv == 0, in which case p == q and the coupling is the diagonal one).
    Complexity: Theta(N) time and space; materializing the dense N x N matrix
    would cost Theta(N^2), which the sparse form avoids.
    """
    m = [min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q)]
    p_leftover = [a - c for a, c in zip(p, m)]
    q_leftover = [b - c for b, c in zip(q, m)]
    d_tv = sum(p_leftover)
    return {"shared": m, "p_leftover": p_leftover, "q_leftover": q_leftover, "d_tv": d_tv}


def dense_maximal_coupling(p: Vec, q: Vec) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Materialize the N x N joint law (for verification on small alphabets)."""
    s = build_maximal_coupling(p, q)
    m, pl, ql, t = s["shared"], s["p_leftover"], s["q_leftover"], s["d_tv"]
    n = len(p)
    c = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for x in range(n):
        c[x][x] += m[x]
    if t > 1e-15:
        for x in range(n):
            if pl[x] == 0.0:
                continue
            for y in range(n):
                c[x][y] += pl[x] * ql[y] / t
    return c


def _alias_cdf(weights: Vec) -> list[float]:
    total, acc, cdf = sum(weights), 0.0, []
    for w in weights:
        acc += w / total
        cdf.append(acc)
    return cdf


def maximal_coupling_sampler(p: Vec, q: Vec, rng: random.Random):
    """Return a zero-argument callable drawing exact samples (X, Y) ~ c*.

    Preprocessing Theta(N); each draw costs Theta(log N) via binary search.
    With probability 1 - d_tv the sampler returns a diagonal pair (x, x);
    otherwise it draws the two coordinates independently from the rescaled
    leftovers, which have disjoint supports, so they never coincide.
    """
    s = build_maximal_coupling(p, q)
    t = float(s["d_tv"])
    cdf_shared = _alias_cdf(s["shared"]) if t < 1.0 else None
    cdf_p = _alias_cdf(s["p_leftover"]) if t > 0.0 else None
    cdf_q = _alias_cdf(s["q_leftover"]) if t > 0.0 else None

    def draw() -> tuple[int, int]:
        if rng.random() >= t and cdf_shared is not None:
            x = bisect.bisect_left(cdf_shared, rng.random())
            return (min(x, len(p) - 1), min(x, len(p) - 1))
        x = bisect.bisect_left(cdf_p, rng.random())
        y = bisect.bisect_left(cdf_q, rng.random())
        return (min(x, len(p) - 1), min(y, len(q) - 1))

    return draw

from __future__ import annotations

from math import factorial
from typing import Iterator, Sequence

Vec = Sequence[float]


def compositions(total: int, parts: int) -> Iterator[tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All non-negative integer vectors of length `parts` summing to `total`."""
    if parts == 1:
        yield (total,)
        return
    for first in range(total + 1):
        for rest in compositions(total - first, parts - 1):
            yield (first,) + rest


def multinomial(counts: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Number of sequences with the given letter counts."""
    num = factorial(sum(counts))
    for c in counts:
        num //= factorial(c)
    return num


def exact_product_tv(p: Vec, q: Vec, n: int) -> float:
    """d_TV(p^{tensor n}, q^{tensor n}) computed exactly.

    Naively this is a sum over |X|^n sequences. Because both product laws are
    exchangeable, all sequences with the same letter-count vector (the same
    *type*) carry the same probability, so the sum collapses to one term per
    type: C(n + N - 1, N - 1) terms instead of N^n. For N = 4, n = 20 that is
    1771 terms rather than 10^12.
    Complexity: Theta(binom(n + N - 1, N - 1) * N).
    """
    n_letters = len(p)
    total = 0.0
    for counts in compositions(n, n_letters):
        weight = multinomial(counts)
        pp = 1.0
        qq = 1.0
        for i, c in enumerate(counts):
            if c:
                pp *= p[i] ** c
                qq *= q[i] ** c
        total += weight * abs(pp - qq)
    return 0.5 * total


def amplification_table(p: Vec, q: Vec, n_max: int) -> list[dict[str, float]]:
    """Exact distance versus the two upper bounds, for n = 1 .. n_max."""
    t = 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))
    rows = []
    for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
        exact = exact_product_tv(p, q, n)
        geometric = 1.0 - (1.0 - t) ** n
        hybrid = n * t
        rows.append({
            "n": float(n),
            "exact": exact,
            "geometric_bound": geometric,
            "hybrid_bound": hybrid,
            "slack": geometric - exact,
            "optimal_error": 0.5 * (1.0 - exact),
            "guaranteed_floor": 0.5 * (1.0 - t) ** n,
        })
    return rows

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence

Mat = Sequence[Sequence[float]]


def shtarkov_optimum(sources: Mat) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Compute the minimax-regret sum and the optimal m-ary decision rule.

    For a family of m laws on an alphabet of size N, the Shtarkov sum is
    C_S = sum_x max_theta p_theta(x). Its logarithm is the minimax regret of
    universal coding; here it is also, exactly, m times one minus the least
    achievable average error of an m-ary decision rule under a uniform prior:
        min_T error(T) = 1 - C_S / m,
    attained by the maximum-likelihood rule T(x) in argmax_theta p_theta(x).
    Complexity: Theta(m N) time, Theta(N) space -- a single sweep, even though
    the quantity it computes is a minimum over m^N decision rules.
    """
    m = len(sources)
    if m == 0:
        raise ValueError("need at least one source")
    n = len(sources[0])
    rule: list[int] = []
    shtarkov = 0.0
    for x in range(n):
        best_theta, best_val = 0, sources[0][x]
        for theta in range(1, m):
            if sources[theta][x] > best_val:
                best_theta, best_val = theta, sources[theta][x]
        rule.append(best_theta)
        shtarkov += best_val
    return {
        "shtarkov_sum": shtarkov,
        "ml_rule": rule,
        "optimal_error": 1.0 - shtarkov / m,
        "guessing_error": 1.0 - 1.0 / m,
        "perfectly_identifiable": abs(shtarkov - m) < 1e-12,
    }


def m_ary_error(sources: Mat, rule: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Uniform-prior average error of an explicit decision rule."""
    m, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    return sum(sources[t][x] for t in range(m) for x in range(n) if rule[x] != t) / m

  const m = p.map((v, i) => Math.min(v, q[i]));
  const ps = p.map((v, i) => v - m[i]), qs = q.map((v, i) => v - m[i]);
  const c = Array.from({length: N}, () => new Array(N).fill(0));

function fit(canvas) {

    ctx.fillText(p[i].toFixed(2), x + bw * 0.29, y0 - hp - 4);

# Sharper Normalization — a guided tour of total variation

> **The one-sentence version.** The factor $\tfrac12$ in
> $d_{TV}(p,q)=\tfrac12\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|$ is not a convention: it is the unique
> normalization that makes this number *equal* to a probability — the best possible
> advantage of a distinguisher, and simultaneously the smallest possible disagreement
> probability of a coupling.

---

## 1. The puzzle

You have two probability distributions on a finite alphabet, say the letters
$a, b, c, d$. Somebody draws one sample from one of them and asks you which. How well
can you do?

Any strategy amounts to picking a set $A$ of letters and saying "it came from $p$"
exactly when the sample lands in $A$. Your **advantage** is
$$\Delta(A) = p(A) - q(A),$$
how much more often you fire on $p$-samples than on $q$-samples. It is $0$ for a useless
test and $1$ for a perfect one.

The first theorem of the tour says that the maximum of $\Delta$ over all $2^{|\mathcal{X}|}$
tests is exactly $d_{TV}(p,q)$, and that you never have to search: the best test is always
$$A^\star = \{x : q(x) \le p(x)\},$$
"bet on $p$ wherever $p$ is likelier". Play with the sliders below and watch the brute-force
maximum over all events track the formula, letter for letter.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof — it is three lines</b></summary>

Write $u_+ = \max(u,0)$. For any event $A$,
$$\sum_{x\in A}(p(x)-q(x)) \;\le\; \sum_{x\in A}(p(x)-q(x))_+ \;\le\; \sum_{x}(p(x)-q(x))_+,$$
discarding the terms that hurt, then adding back the ones that help. And because both laws
sum to $1$, the total surplus of $p$ over $q$ equals the total deficit:
$$\sum_x (p(x)-q(x))_+ \;=\; \sum_x (q(x)-p(x))_+ \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)| \;=\; d_{TV}(p,q).$$
Both inequalities become equalities at $A = A^\star$. That symmetry between surplus and deficit
**is** the factor $\tfrac12$; the $\ell^1$ norm simply counts both.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Background: why randomizing your test cannot help</b></summary>

A randomized test accepts $x$ with probability $g(x)\in[0,1]$. Its advantage
$\sum_x (p(x)-q(x))g(x)$ is a *linear* function of $g$ on the cube $[0,1]^{\mathcal{X}}$, and a
linear function on a cube is maximized at a vertex — a deterministic test. So coin flips buy
nothing, and $d_{TV}$ caps every test, deterministic or not. More generally, for any observable
$g$ with values in $[m,M]$,
$$|\mathbb{E}_p[g]-\mathbb{E}_q[g]| \le (M-m)\,d_{TV}(p,q),$$
which is exactly the statement "distributions $\varepsilon$-close in total variation agree to
within $\varepsilon$ on every bounded metric".
</details>

---

## 2. Where the notorious factor of two actually lives

If you insist on $\|p-q\|_1$, you are not wrong — you are answering a different question.
Enlarge the class of tests from $g:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]$ to *signed* tests
$g:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1]$, and the optimum doubles:

| test class | attained optimum |
|---|---|
| $g:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]$ (probabilistic) | $d_{TV}(p,q)$ |
| $g:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1]$ (signed) | $2\,d_{TV}(p,q)=\|p-q\|_1$ |

The two cubes are related by the affine map $g\mapsto(1+g)/2$, and since
$\sum_x(p(x)-q(x))=0$ the additive shift is invisible while the scaling by $\tfrac12$ survives.
The $\ell^1$ answer is the *correct* answer to the coarser question. Only one of the two is
the probability of anything.

---

## 3. The dual picture: making two random variables agree

Here is the turn that always feels like magic. A **coupling** of $p$ and $q$ is a joint law
on pairs $(X,Y)$ with $X\sim p$ and $Y\sim q$ — a way of running the two worlds side by side,
correlated however you like. How often can you force $X = Y$?

$$\boxed{\ \min_{\text{couplings}} \mathbb{P}[X\neq Y] \;=\; d_{TV}(p,q) \;=\; \max_{A}\bigl(p(A)-q(A)\bigr)\ }$$

The same number, from opposite directions, with explicit optima on both sides. The heat map in
panel 3 of the widget above is the optimal transport plan: bright diagonal = agreement,
everything off it = disagreement, and the off-diagonal mass is exactly $d_{TV}$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal both halves of the proof</b></summary>

**No coupling can do better.** For any coupling $c$ and any event $A$,
$$p(A)-q(A) = \mathbb{E}_c[\mathbf{1}_A(X) - \mathbf{1}_A(Y)] \le \mathbb{P}_c[X\neq Y],$$
because the bracket vanishes when $X=Y$ and never exceeds $1$. Feed in the *best* event
$A^\star$ and the left side becomes $d_{TV}$. The optimal event is the certificate for the
coupling bound — that is what "dual" means here.

**Some coupling achieves it.** Let $m(x)=\min(p(x),q(x))$ be the shared mass, of total
$1 - d_{TV}$, and let $p^\sharp = p-m$, $q^\sharp = q-m$ be the leftovers, each of total
$d_{TV}$. Set
$$c^\star(x,y) = m(x)\,[x=y] + \frac{p^\sharp(x)\,q^\sharp(y)}{d_{TV}}.$$
Put all shared mass on the diagonal; pair the leftovers independently, rescaled. The marginals
work out because each leftover totals exactly $d_{TV}$, and at every letter at most one of
$p^\sharp(x), q^\sharp(x)$ is nonzero — so the second term contributes nothing to the diagonal
and the disagreement probability is exactly $d_{TV}$.
</details>

## 4. Cashing it in: four things sharpness buys

An *attained* bound survives composition; a merely valid one leaks a constant at every step.

**(a) The best possible hypothesis test.** Nature flips a fair coin, draws from $p$ or $q$, and
you must guess. The least achievable average error is exactly
$$\frac{1-d_{TV}(p,q)}{2}.$$
With the $\ell^1$ normalization the same formula reads $(1-\|p-q\|_1)/2$, which is *negative*
whenever the laws are more than half apart — a lower bound on a probability that is negative is
not a theorem.

**(b) Processing cannot create information.** Push both laws through any stochastic channel —
a feature map, a quantizer, added noise, a neural network — and the distance can only shrink:
$d_{TV}(pK, qK)\le d_{TV}(p,q)$. Privacy engineers read it from right to left.

**(c) Many samples buy a geometric, not a linear, advantage.**
$$d_{TV}(p^{\otimes n}, q^{\otimes n}) \le 1-(1-d_{TV}(p,q))^n,$$
proved by coupling each coordinate maximally and independently. Unlike the textbook bound
$n\,d_{TV}$, it never leaves $[0,1]$, and it is strictly better for every $n\ge2$. Its
consequence is a sample-complexity floor that never goes vacuous: after $n$ draws, every test
still errs with probability at least $\tfrac12(1-d_{TV})^n$.

Play the guessing game yourself — set the two sources, choose $n$, and watch a Monte Carlo
simulation of the maximum-likelihood rule converge onto the theoretical optimum while the
hybrid bound collapses:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why the exponential rate is the honest one</b></summary>

Under the maximal coupling, with probability $1-d_{TV}$ the two worlds emit the *same* letter,
and on that event no test can possibly tell them apart. Over $n$ independent coordinates all of
them coincide with probability $(1-d_{TV})^n$, and on that event you are reduced to a coin flip.
Hence error $\ge\tfrac12(1-d_{TV})^n\approx\tfrac12 e^{-n\,d_{TV}}$: you need $n\asymp 1/d_{TV}$
samples before you can hope to win, and no fewer, ever.
</details>

**(d) From divergence control to test control.** Practitioners control the Kullback–Leibler
divergence, not total variation. Pinsker's inequality $d_{TV}\le\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}/2}$, composed
with the event characterization, turns an analytic quantity into an operational guarantee: *no*
event and *no* test separates the two hypotheses by more than $\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}/2}$. And the
converse is an audit tool: a single observed separating event certifies
$\mathrm{KL}\ge 2\,\Delta(A)^2$.

---

## 5. A coincidence that isn't

Universal compression has its own scalar for a family of $m$ candidate sources: the Shtarkov sum
$C_S=\sum_x\max_\theta p_\theta(x)$, whose logarithm is the price in bits of not knowing which
source you face. Statistics has its own scalar: the least average error of an $m$-way decision
rule. They are the same number.

$$\min_{T}\ \mathrm{err}(T)\;=\;1-\frac{C_S}{m},$$

attained by maximum likelihood. For $m=2$ one has $C_S = 1 + d_{TV}$ and the formula collapses
to $(1-d_{TV})/2$ — the two-point bound, recovered on the nose from a compression quantity.

{{algorithm:3}}

## 7. Where this goes next

The geometric amplification law is sharp compared with the linear bound but is still *not the
truth*: the exact $n$-sample distance sits strictly below it, because a product of maximal
couplings need not be maximal. Closing the gap needs a quantity that multiplies exactly over
products — the Hellinger affinity $\rho(p,q)=\sum_x\sqrt{p(x)q(x)}$, which satisfies
$\rho(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})=\rho(p,q)^n$ exactly, and is tied to total variation by the
sandwich $1-\rho\le d_{TV}\le\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$. Total variation is the natural currency of
testing; affinity is the natural currency of tensorization; the exchange rate between them is
the next chapter.

# Operational consequences of the sharp total-variation normalization

`MachineLearning.TotalVariation.EventSup` proved the factor-`1/2` characterization

`d_TV(p, q) = max_{A} (p(A) − q(A))`.

Here we cash it in.  Three classical pillars of statistical learning theory are
derived, each of them *tight* precisely because the normalization is the sharp
one:

1. **Le Cam's two-point bound.**  For the uniform-prior binary testing problem
   `p` vs `q`, the Bayes error of the best test is exactly `(1 − d_TV)/2`
   (`isLeast_bayesError`).  With the crude `ℓ¹` normalization one would only get
   the vacuous `(1 − ‖p − q‖₁)/2`, which is negative as soon as `‖p − q‖₁ > 1`.
2. **Data processing.**  Post-processing by an arbitrary stochastic channel — in
   particular by any deterministic feature map / statistic — cannot increase
   total variation (`tvDist_channel_le`, `tvDist_map_le`).
3. **Tensorization and sample complexity.**  `d_TV(p^{⊗n}, q^{⊗n}) ≤ n·d_TV(p, q)`
   (`tvDist_powLaw_le`), so a learner needs `n ≳ 1/d_TV` i.i.d. samples before it
   can tell the two sources apart at all (`bayesError_powLaw_ge`).

## Main results

* `bayesError_eq_half_one_add_eventGap`, `isLeast_bayesError`,
  `bayesError_ge_half_one_sub_tvDist` — Le Cam;
* `tvDist_channel_le`, `tvDist_map_le` — the data-processing inequality;
* `tvDist_prodLaw_le` — two-factor tensorization (hybrid argument);
* `tvDist_powLaw_le` — the `n`-sample bound by induction;
* `bayesError_powLaw_ge` — the resulting sample-complexity lower bound.

## Application keywords

Le Cam method, hypothesis testing, data processing inequality, tensorization,
sample complexity, indistinguishability, hybrid argument
